articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.

This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions related to Iran, though specific details of the changes were not immediately released. General Licenses typically permit certain categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other specific activities.

The issuance of an amended General License indicates a recalibration of U.S. sanctions policy towards Iran, potentially adjusting the scope of permissible activities for U.S. persons or in U.S. jurisdiction.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Linked to North Korea and DRC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

For North Korea, the designations targeted 10 individuals and one entity for allegedly supporting government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes that defraud U.S. companies and generate revenue for North Korea's weapons and missile programs. Four individuals were designated under Executive Order (E.O.) 13687, while the entity and six individuals were designated under E.O. 13722.

These actions build on previous efforts to disrupt illicit revenue streams for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) and are part of a coordinated international effort with Australia and the European Union to counter North Korea's use of overseas workers and malicious cyber activities. The designations also included actions related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, though specific details of those designations were not immediately available.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement with OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026. The settlement amount was $1,529,685.

The settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs. Concurrently, the Department of Justice announced a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., under which the company will pay $975,721.84 in criminal penalties.

OFAC credited $487,861 of Extreme Networks' payment to the Justice Department against its settlement, resulting in $1,041,824 owed directly to OFAC. The company's disclosure was not timely, coming under imminent threat of public disclosure, but full cooperation and remediation were noted.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments aim to provide updated guidance and clarification for financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC regulations. The FAQs typically address common compliance questions and offer practical advice on navigating complex sanctions requirements.

The revisions reflect OFAC's ongoing efforts to ensure clarity and effectiveness in sanctions compliance, helping regulated entities to better understand and implement their responsibilities in preventing illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 21, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, removals from the Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists, and the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, along with amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations target individuals and entities involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security interests. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain individuals and entities from its Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists, indicating a recalibration of these specific sanctions measures.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia, alongside updated FAQs, suggests an effort to refine the scope of permissible activities under these sanctions programs, potentially to facilitate certain transactions or provide clearer guidance to the public.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, along with the issuance of associated General Licenses.

These designations target individuals and entities deemed to be involved in activities that threaten American intellectual property, reflecting a continued commitment to safeguarding U.S. innovation and economic security.

The accompanying General Licenses aim to mitigate any unintended consequences of these designations, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions that might otherwise be prohibited, ensuring that legitimate activities can continue.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026.

This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela, potentially adjusting the scope of permissible activities for U.S. persons or within U.S. jurisdiction. The Venezuelan government, including PdVSA, remains blocked under E.O. 13884, but OFAC has issued broad general licenses for the oil, gas, and mining sectors since January 2026.

The issuance of an amended General License and FAQ indicates a refinement of U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, aiming to provide clearer guidance and potentially facilitate certain transactions while maintaining overall sanctions pressure.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations targeted 16 individuals in Iran and the UAE and 10 entities—eight in Iran, one in Iraq, and one in Hong Kong—for their roles in Iran's international financial networks and shadow banking activities, under Executive Order 13902 as part of Operation Economic Outcast. OFAC also issued General License FF, authorizing qualifying wind-down transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance through October 30, 2026.

The Cuba designation adds to the existing comprehensive embargo against the country, which has been in place since the 1960s. The new and amended General Licenses and FAQs aim to provide clarity and specific authorizations for certain transactions, while maintaining the overall pressure of the sanctions regimes.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Lewis Baach Kaufmann Middlemiss

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Individual from Venezuela-Related Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Venezuela sanctions program on October 14, 2026.

This delisting indicates a potential shift in U.S. policy regarding specific individuals previously sanctioned in connection with the Venezuelan government. Such removals can occur due to various factors, including changes in the individual's activities, a reassessment of their role, or diplomatic considerations.
The removal of an individual from the SDN List typically means that U.S. persons are no longer prohibited from engaging in transactions with that individual, provided no other sanctions apply.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Lewis Baach Kaufmann Middlemiss

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026.

These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit narcotics trafficking and terrorism financing, underscoring the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting these dangerous networks. On this date, OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against four individuals and 11 entities, all in Mexico, for supporting Cartel del Noreste through businesses involved in horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector.

The actions aim to sever their access to the international financial system and prevent them from facilitating further illicit activities, thereby protecting U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Lewis Baach Kaufmann Middlemiss

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026.

This penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions failures.

OFAC's settlement resolves 475 apparent violations, totaling approximately $14.83 million, that occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, spanning sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The violations included payments via blocked banks, flaws in alert prioritization, delays in watchlist updates, and account mishandling.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This marks the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with systemic breakdowns in internal controls. The bank's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to numerous late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

This action is coordinated with a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and an $11.6 million settlement from the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for related AML and sanctions failures. The OCC's penalty will be paid to the U.S. Treasury.
articles.source: OCC / U.S. Treasury / Foley Hoag LLP

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training.

The bank's risk assessment failed to adequately address risks in its credit and charge card products, focusing instead on its demand deposit business. This resulted in a failure to timely identify, evaluate, and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. This action was taken in coordination with a concurrent cease-and-desist order by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Former Fifth Third Bank Teller for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued an Order of Prohibition against Jennifer Hamblin, a former Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A.

The prohibition order was issued due to Hamblin's embezzlement of approximately $292,000 in customer funds. Such actions reinforce the OCC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for their conduct regarding the affairs of a bank.

Orders of Prohibition prevent an individual from participating in the affairs of any bank or other institution as defined in 12 U.S.C. 1818(e)(7), serving as a deterrent against violations and breaches of fiduciary duty.

articles.headline: DHS Adds Three Entities to UFLPA Entity List for Forced Labor in Xinjiang
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as Chair of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), announced the addition of three entities to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List, effective October 29, 2026.

These additions target entities working with the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR) to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or members of persecuted groups out of Xinjiang. The newly listed entities are Baoding LYSZD Trade And Business Co., Ltd., Hetian Haolin Hair Accessories Co. Ltd. (and two aliases), and Hetian Taida Apparel Co., Ltd (and one alias).

This update supersedes the UFLPA Entity List published in the Federal Register on August 3, 2026, and brings the total number of entities on the list to 187, marking the largest single expansion since the UFLPA took effect in 2022. The UFLPA Entity List identifies entities for which there is a rebuttable presumption that goods mined, produced, or manufactured by them were made with forced labor.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
